name: Pakistan
summary: The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) licenses and supervises banks, DFIs and microfinance banks and is their AML/CFT/CPF supervisor under the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010. The Financial Monitoring Unit receives suspicious and currency transaction reports. Targeted financial sanctions come from Ministry of Foreign Affairs orders (UN listings) and NACTA/Ministry of Interior proscriptions. SECP adds governance rules for listed banks, the Banking Mohtasib hears customer complaints, and FBR runs FATCA/CRS reporting. Section 7G of the AML Act requires training programmes, and SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations require an annual, needs-based training programme for staff, management and the board, with periodic testing. The 2025 Business Conduct and Fair Treatment of Consumers framework requires regular conduct training. Most other areas are competence or framework obligations.

regulators.name: State Bank of Pakistan
regulators.role: Central bank, licensing authority and prudential, conduct and AML/CFT/CPF supervisor of banks, DFIs and microfinance banks; issues regulations, frameworks and circulars.

regulators.name: Financial Monitoring Unit
regulators.role: Pakistan's financial intelligence unit under the AML Act 2010; receives STRs and CTRs through goAML and issues reporting guidelines and red flags.

regulators.name: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
regulators.role: Corporate and capital-market regulator; its Code of Corporate Governance Regulations apply to listed companies, including listed banks.

regulators.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs
regulators.role: Gives effect to UN Security Council sanctions through SROs under the United Nations (Security Council) Act 1948 and the Freezing and Seizure Order 2019.

regulators.name: National Counter Terrorism Authority
regulators.role: Maintains the domestic list of proscribed organisations and persons under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 and related CFT guidance.

regulators.name: Banking Mohtasib Pakistan
regulators.role: Statutory banking ombudsman under Part IVA of the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962; hears customer complaints against banks after the bank has had 45 days to respond.

regulators.name: Federal Board of Revenue
regulators.role: Tax authority; competent authority for automatic exchange of information (CRS and FATCA enrolment and reporting by financial institutions).

regulators.name: Federal Ombudsperson for Protection against Harassment
regulators.role: Hears workplace harassment complaints under the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP AML/CFT/CPF Regulations: Annual AML Training
programs.why: SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, issued under section 6A(2) of the AML Act 2010, require an annual training programme built on a yearly training needs assessment. It must include sessions for sponsor shareholders, the board, senior and line management and field staff. Staff with AML/CFT/CPF duties must learn current laundering and terrorist-financing methods and their TFS, CDD and STR duties, and their knowledge must be tested periodically. Computer-based or online training and tests are expected, especially for front-end staff. Section 7G of the AML Act also requires training programmes.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering, Combating the Financing of Terrorism & Countering Proliferation Financing (AML/CFT/CPF) Regulations (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2020)
references.note: Issued under section 6A(2) of the AML Act 2010; replaced the 2019 AML/CFT Regulations for banks and DFIs. Contains the annual training programme and periodic staff testing requirements.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (as amended up to September 2020)
references.note: Every reporting entity must have compliance arrangements that include a management-level compliance officer and training programmes proportionate to its ML/TF risks and size.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Annual training programme after a yearly training needs assessment, covering sponsor shareholders, the board, management and field staff; content kept current; periodic staff testing; computer-based or online training for front-end staff.

references.title: Guidelines for Training and Development of Bank Employees (BPRD Circular No. 12 of 2016)
references.note: Banks need a board-approved training policy, a training budget approved annually, training MIS for SBP inspectors and function-specific e-learning in critical areas such as AML/CFT.

references.title: SBP press release on the Guidelines for Training and Development of Bank Employees (30 September 2016)
references.note: Summarises the 2016 guidelines: a board-approved training policy built on training needs assessment, an annual board-approved training budget, and attention to staff in remote and rural branches; compliance was due by 31 December 2016.

programs.title: Pakistan | Countering Terrorist Financing under the AML Act and ATA 1997
programs.why: The SBP Regulations cover terrorist financing alongside money laundering. They require the annual programme to teach responsible staff current terrorist-financing techniques and trends. Terrorist financing is an offence under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, and the AML Act requires an STR when a transaction may involve it. Staff need to recognise these risks, including those involving proscribed persons and organisations.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Training for staff responsible for AML/CFT/CPF must cover terrorist-financing methods and trends.

references.title: The Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
references.note: Proscription, the terrorist-financing offences (fund raising, use and possession, funding arrangements, money laundering) and the freezing duty.

programs.title: Pakistan | Countering Proliferation Financing (SBP CPF Requirements)
programs.why: Since 2020, SBP's regulations explicitly add countering proliferation financing to the AML/CFT regime, and the required training is for staff with AML/CFT/CPF responsibilities. UN proliferation-related sanctions are applied through MoFA orders under the United Nations (Security Council) Act 1948. Staff need to understand the asset-freeze and prohibition duties that apply to those designations.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2020)
references.note: Extended the regulations to countering proliferation financing, including the training requirement.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: TFS duties cover persons designated under the UNSC Act, and the annual training programme must give special emphasis to TFS for both terrorist and proliferation financing.

references.title: UNSC Sanctions (SROs under the United Nations (Security Council) Act, 1948)
references.note: MoFA publishes the SROs that give domestic effect to UN sanctions committee listings.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework and KYC
programs.why: In July 2025 SBP brought its account-opening and onboarding instructions together in one framework. It sets the documents and steps for each customer and account type, and it relies on the AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for the CDD standard itself. Under those regulations, AML/CFT/CPF training must cover staff CDD duties, so onboarding staff need to know both the procedures and their purpose.

references.title: Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2025)
references.note: Single framework for onboarding requirements; regulated entities had three months to comply.

references.title: Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework (framework text)
references.note: Covers branch and remote onboarding of individuals and entities by banks, DFIs, MFBs, digital banks and EMIs, with sections on identity verification, sanctions screening and EDD; reliance on third-party CDD follows Regulation 3 of the AML/CFT/CPF Regulations.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Training content must address staff CDD obligations.

programs.title: Pakistan | Customer Due Diligence under AML Act s.7A-7D and SBP Regulation 2
programs.why: The 2020 amendments put CDD duties into the AML Act itself. A reporting entity that cannot complete CDD must decline or end the relationship and consider filing an STR. SBP's Regulation 2 sets out the detailed CDD rules, and the regulations require the training programme to cover CDD obligations. Staff therefore need practical CDD training, including what to do when CDD fails.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (as amended up to September 2020)
references.note: Statutory CDD duties of reporting entities, including what to do when CDD cannot be completed.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Detailed CDD requirements for SBP regulated entities; the training content must include staff CDD duties (Regulation 13(14)).

programs.title: Pakistan | Enhanced Due Diligence for High-Risk Customers (SBP)
programs.why: The SBP Regulations and SBP's risk-based approach guidelines require enhanced measures for higher-risk customers, relationships and geographies. Applying them takes informed judgement from relationship and compliance staff. No separate EDD course is prescribed; it falls within the general AML/CFT/CPF training duty.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: EDD is required for higher-risk customers and situations and can include senior-management approval.

references.title: AML/CFT Guidelines on Risk Based Approach (RBA) for Banks/DFIs/MFBs
references.note: Guidance on applying risk-based measures; says AML/CFT training should be high quality, obligatory for relevant staff, tailored by business line, tested and ongoing.

programs.title: Pakistan | Ongoing Monitoring and CDD Review (SBP Regulations)
programs.why: Under the SBP Regulations, CDD continues after onboarding. Banks must monitor relationships over time, keep customer data up to date and follow set rules for dormant accounts, defined as accounts with no customer-initiated activity for a year. The 2022 amendments revised those dormant-account rules. Staff must understand when a customer profile has to be refreshed or escalated, but no stand-alone course is mandated.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Ongoing monitoring of business relationships and the dormant-account rules, including notices one month, seven days and one day before an account is marked dormant.

references.title: BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022 (amendments to AML/CFT/CPF Regulations)
references.note: Revised the treatment of dormant accounts within the ongoing CDD rules.

programs.title: Pakistan | Beneficial Ownership Identification (SBP AML/CFT/CPF)
programs.why: Banks must identify and verify the natural persons who own or control customers that are legal persons or arrangements. FMU red flags on misuse of legal persons show the typologies staff should recognise. This is a CDD competence within the general training duty.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: CDD for legal persons and arrangements includes identifying beneficial owners.

references.title: Red Flag Indicators for Misuse of Legal Persons
references.note: Indicators such as round-tripping and activity outside the declared business profile.

programs.title: Pakistan | Politically Exposed Persons under SBP AML/CFT/CPF Regulations
programs.why: Regulation 5 of the SBP Regulations deals with PEPs and their family members and close associates. Banks must identify them, obtain senior-management approval, establish source of wealth and funds and monitor the relationship more closely. Staff must recognise PEP relationships and escalate them correctly, but no separate PEP course is prescribed.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: PEPs, family members and close associates: detection before and during the relationship, senior-management approval, source of wealth and funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring.

programs.title: Pakistan | Sanctions Screening against UNSC and Proscribed Lists
programs.why: Banks must screen customers and transactions against UN listings published by MoFA and against domestic proscriptions maintained by NACTA and the Ministry of Interior. These lists change often, through new MoFA SROs and updated proscription lists. Screening staff need to know where each list comes from and how to handle a potential match.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Real-time screening of customers with an effective name-screening solution and sufficient trained resources, ongoing monitoring and careful analysis of potential matches.

references.title: UNSC Sanctions (SRO portal and committee listings)
references.note: MoFA issues an SRO whenever a UN sanctions committee adds, removes or amends a listing.

references.title: Proscribed Persons
references.note: Domestic list of persons placed on the Fourth Schedule of the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997.

programs.title: Pakistan | Targeted Financial Sanctions under UNSC Act 1948 and ATA 1997
programs.why: The SBP Regulations require training to cover staff obligations on targeted financial sanctions. Banks must freeze, without delay or prior notice, funds of persons designated under the UNSC Act 1948 or proscribed under the ATA 1997, and of those acting for them. They must not make funds available to such persons, must report freezes and attempted transactions to the FMU, and must tell SBP within 48 hours. SBP's TFS FAQs read 'without delay' as generally within 24 hours.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Freeze without delay or prior notice, report to FMU, report freezes to SBP within 48 hours, and train staff on their TFS duties.

references.title: United Nations Security Council (Freezing and Seizure) Order, 2019
references.note: Freeze covers property owned or controlled by designated persons; frozen property cannot be used without written approval of the authorised agency.

references.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on Targeted Financial Sanctions
references.note: SBP guidance to regulated entities on applying UN and domestic TFS; treats "without delay" as generally within 24 hours.

references.title: The Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
references.note: Property of proscribed organisations and persons must be frozen without prior notice and without delay, with a report within 48 hours of the freeze.

programs.title: Pakistan | Suspicious Transaction Reporting to FMU (AML Act s.7)
programs.why: Under section 7 of the AML Act, a reporting entity must promptly file an STR with the FMU when it knows or suspects that a transaction involves crime proceeds or terrorist financing. Tipping off is a criminal offence under section 34. FMU's STR and CTR Reporting Regulations 2025 repeat the prompt-filing duty through goAML and require risk-based procedures to detect suspicious activity. The SBP Regulations require training on analysing unusual transactions and alerts for possible STRs. FMU guidance explains STR-F and STR-A reports and acknowledgements.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (as amended up to September 2020)
references.note: STR duty, to be met promptly; when CDD cannot be completed or would tip off the customer, an STR is to be considered or filed; tipping off is a criminal offence.

references.title: Guidelines for the Reporting Entities on filing of Suspicious Transaction Reports
references.note: How to prepare and file STRs on goAML, choose indicators and keep acceptance acknowledgements.

references.title: Suspicious Transaction and Currency Transaction Reporting Regulations, 2025
references.note: Replaced the AML Regulations 2015; STRs go to the FMU through goAML promptly once suspicion forms, entities need risk-based detection procedures, and staff must not disclose that a report was made.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Training must cover analysis of out-of-pattern transactions and alerts for possible STRs; the ban on tipping off must be part of the code of ethics signed at induction.

programs.title: Pakistan | Identifying Unusual Transactions (FMU Red Flags for Banks)
programs.why: SBP-required training must prepare staff to analyse unusual transactions and alerts for possible STRs. The FMU publishes red flags for banks, such as structuring and transfers to or from financial secrecy havens. It issues further red-flag circulars, including a June 2026 circular on corruption-related laundering. Training content must be kept current with FMU guidance, which the regulations name as an input.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Training must cover analysis of abnormal or out-of-pattern transactions and the alerts they generate.

references.title: Red flags for identification of Suspicious Transactions for Banks
references.note: Bank-specific indicators of possible money laundering or terrorist financing.

references.title: FMU Circulars
references.note: Lists 2026 circulars on red flags for corruption-related money laundering (24 June 2026) and on STR-G reporting for government entities on goAML (28 July 2026).

programs.title: Pakistan | Correspondent Banking Due Diligence (SBP Regulations)
audience: Financial institutions and correspondent banking teams
programs.why: The SBP Regulations have a dedicated correspondent-banking regulation. It requires due diligence on respondent institutions, senior-management approval and controls against shell banks. The teams that manage these relationships need to apply it competently, but no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Correspondent banking: information on respondents, senior-management approval, EDD and a ban on shell-bank relationships.

programs.title: Pakistan | AML/CFT Risk-Based Approach and National Risk Assessment
programs.why: SBP expects banks to assess their own ML/TF/PF risks and calibrate controls, drawing on Pakistan's national risk assessment. The RBA guidelines say AML/CFT training should be compulsory for relevant staff, tailored by business line, tested and ongoing rather than one-off. Those guidelines are guidance, so the topic is treated as a competence requirement.

references.title: AML/CFT Guidelines on Risk Based Approach (RBA) for Banks/DFIs/MFBs
references.note: Explains entity risk assessment, risk-based controls and features of effective staff training.

references.title: Summarized National Risk Assessment 2023
references.note: Public summary of Pakistan's national ML/TF risk assessment, used as input to bank risk assessments.

programs.title: Pakistan | AML Record Keeping and CTR Reporting (10-Year Retention)
programs.why: The AML Act requires STR and CTR records to be kept for at least ten years, and CDD and transaction records for at least five. The SBP Regulations go further: ten years after the relationship ends for CDD records and ten years after completion for transaction records. Under FMU's 2025 reporting regulations, CTRs for cash transactions at or above the set threshold are due within seven working days. Operations staff need to know these rules, though no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (as amended up to September 2020)
references.note: CTRs due within seven working days; STR and CTR records kept for at least ten years; CDD and transaction records kept for at least five years under the Act.

references.title: Guidelines for the Reporting Entities on filing of Currency Transaction Reports
references.note: How reporting entities file CTRs with the FMU.

references.title: Suspicious Transaction and Currency Transaction Reporting Regulations, 2025
references.note: Cash transactions at or above the threshold set by the National Executive Committee are reported on goAML within seven working days, subject to listed exemptions.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: CDD records kept ten years after the relationship ends; transaction, STR and CTR records kept at least ten years from completion.

programs.title: Pakistan | AML/CFT/CPF Training for Branch and Field Staff
programs.why: The SBP Regulations name field staff among those the annual training programme must reach. They require periodic knowledge testing and computer-based or online AML/CFT/CPF/TFS training, noting that front-end staff are the first contact with customers. SBP's 2016 training guidelines also ask banks to give staff in remote and rural branches enough training each year. Branch staff are the first line for CDD, unusual activity and TFS screening.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: Annual programme must include field staff; periodic testing; computer-based or online training and tests, stressed for front-end staff.

references.title: Guidelines for Training and Development of Bank Employees (BPRD Circular No. 12 of 2016)
references.note: Training for remote-area branch staff and AML/CFT e-learning available to all employees.

references.title: SBP press release on the Guidelines for Training and Development of Bank Employees (30 September 2016)
references.note: Summarises the 2016 guidelines: a board-approved training policy built on training needs assessment, an annual board-approved training budget, and attention to staff in remote and rural branches; compliance was due by 31 December 2016.

programs.title: Pakistan | AML/CFT/CPF Oversight for Board and Senior Management
programs.why: The SBP Regulations make the board ultimately responsible for effective AML/CFT/CPF controls. They also name sponsor shareholders, the board and senior management as groups the annual training programme must cover. Leaders need to understand their oversight role, risk appetite and the AML/CFT Sanctions Rules 2020 that SBP enforces.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2020)
references.note: Board holds ultimate responsibility; the training programme must cover sponsors, the board and senior management.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: The board holds ultimate responsibility for effective AML/CFT/CPF controls; the annual programme must include sessions for sponsor shareholders, the board and senior management.

programs.title: Pakistan | Anti-Bribery and Corruption Awareness for Bank Staff
programs.why: No SBP rule prescribing anti-bribery training for bank staff was verified. Corruption is a predicate offence for money laundering, however. The FMU issued a June 2026 circular on red flags linking corruption and laundering, and the Banking Mohtasib's jurisdiction under the Banking Companies Ordinance includes complaints of corruption, nepotism and maladministration by banks. Awareness training is therefore good practice.

references.title: FMU Circulars
references.note: Lists FMU Circular No. 01 of 2026 (24 June 2026) on red flags for corruption-related money laundering.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Fraud Risk Management and Digital Fraud Controls
programs.why: SBP requires a board-approved fraud prevention policy that sets out staff roles in preventing, detecting, investigating and reporting fraud. Material frauds must be reported to SBP within set deadlines, and staff are accountable for late reporting. The 2023 digital banking security measures add controls and a liability shift that makes banks compensate customers for delays. Staff must know these procedures, but no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions on Fraud Risk Management for Banks/MFBs/DFIs
references.note: Board-approved fraud prevention policy setting the roles of staff and others in preventing, detecting, investigating and reporting fraud; quarterly fraud review by a board committee; frauds of Rs 5 million or more go to the board.

references.title: Fraud Risk Management and Reporting (BPRD Circular No. 03 of 2014)
references.note: Reporting timelines for material frauds and staff accountability for delayed reporting.

references.title: Measures to Enhance Security of Digital Banking Products and Services (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2023)
references.note: Digital fraud controls and a liability shift requiring prompt compensation where banks miss deadlines.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Corporate Governance Regulatory Framework
programs.why: SBP's 2021 Corporate Governance Regulatory Framework brings together governance requirements for banks and DFIs. It strengthens the board's role and sets fit and proper criteria for sponsors, directors, CEOs and key executives. No general staff training is prescribed, but governance roles require competence in the framework.

references.title: Corporate Governance Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2021)
references.note: Consolidated governance and fit and proper requirements for banks and DFIs.

programs.title: Pakistan | Directors' Orientation and Directors' Training Program
programs.why: Listed banks fall under SECP's Code of Corporate Governance Regulations 2019. These require director orientation on the regulations, applicable laws and directors' duties. A new director should obtain directors' training certification within one year, unless exempt by experience. For microfinance banks, SBP rules require first-year director training on governance, IT, cybersecurity and AML/CFT. SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations also include the board in the annual training programme.

references.title: Listed Companies (Code of Corporate Governance) Regulations, 2019
references.issuer: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
references.note: Director orientation, and directors' training certification for new directors within one year of appointment.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Microfinance Banks (updated May 16, 2025)
references.note: MFB directors must attend training on corporate governance, IT, cybersecurity and AML/CFT within their first year, unless already trained or experienced on a foreign corporate board.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Fit and Proper Test for Directors and Key Executives
programs.why: SBP's fit and proper test assesses integrity, track record, solvency, qualifications, experience and conflicts of interest. It applies to sponsors, board members, the CEO and key executives, and changes must be reported on an ongoing basis. These are competence requirements rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: Corporate Governance Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2021)
references.note: Revised fit and proper criteria and proforma for sponsors, directors, CEOs and key executives.

programs.title: Pakistan | Code of Conduct and Responsible Business Conduct (SBP BC&FRF)
programs.why: SBP's Business Conduct and Fair Treatment of Consumers Regulatory Framework requires a code of conduct for employees, including third-party staff, with disciplinary action for breaches. Banks must run regular training and awareness sessions on responsible conduct for staff at all levels, under an annual training plan whose modules cover the code of conduct. FTC deliverables must feed into staff KPIs. The AML/CFT/CPF Regulations also require the ban on tipping off to be written into the code of ethics that employees and directors sign at induction.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Employee code of conduct including third-party staff, FTC goals in KPIs, regular training and awareness sessions, and an annual training plan whose modules cover the code of conduct and discipline for mis-selling and fraud.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for SBP Regulated Entities, updated to 28 November 2022 (Annex-B to BPRD Circular Letter No. 33 of 2022)
references.note: The ban on disclosing that an STR has been filed must be part of the code of ethics signed by employees and directors at induction.

programs.title: Pakistan | Whistle-Blowing Programme (SBP Fraud Risk Instructions)
programs.why: SBP's fraud risk management instructions advise banks to run a board-approved whistle-blowing programme so that staff and outsiders can raise concerns without fear of reprisal. Staff must know the channel exists and how it protects them for it to work. No separate training is prescribed.

references.title: Instructions on Fraud Risk Management for Banks/MFBs/DFIs
references.note: Advises a board-approved whistle-blowing programme so staff and others can raise concerns without fear of reprisal, with a designated unit or committee to handle complaints.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers Framework (BC&FRF)
programs.why: The BC&FRF, issued in October 2025, sets outcome-based principles in Part I and six pillars in Part II: governance, disclosure, fair treatment, data protection, dispute resolution, and awareness and capacity building. It requires regular training and awareness sessions for employees at all levels, including third-party staff. Under the capacity-building pillar, banks need a training policy and an annual training plan with refresher courses, separate programmes for new and existing staff, and training on new SBP instructions and digital fraud.

references.title: BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers Regulatory Framework
references.note: Effective immediately except the governance pillar, which applies from 1 January 2026; circulars in Annexure-A are withdrawn.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework
references.note: Regular training for employees including third-party staff, and an annual training plan with refresher courses and separate programmes for new and existing staff.

references.title: SBP press release on the BC&FRF (17 October 2025)
references.note: Summarises the two-part structure and six pillars.

programs.title: Pakistan | Fair Treatment of Consumers Outcomes under BC&FRF
programs.why: Fair treatment of consumers is the core of the BC&FRF. Banks must ensure staff are trained, competent and monitored on responsible conduct and FTC, and must train employees, including third-party staff, regularly. The board approves the FTC framework and oversees conduct risk through a board committee. The framework still requires banks to apply SBP's Conduct Assessment Framework from 2016, as amended.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Staff must be trained, competent and monitored on responsible conduct and FTC; regular training for employees including third-party staff.

programs.title: Pakistan | Responsible Lending and Fair Conduct in Credit (BC&FRF)
programs.why: The BC&FRF requires banks to design and sell products in line with customers' needs, risk tolerance and financial capacity, to disclose terms clearly and to follow fair financing and recovery practices. It bans harassment by recovery staff and requires banks to engage suitably qualified collection staff and give them the training they need. That is an explicit duty for collection teams; for other credit staff this is a competence requirement.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Products designed around customer needs and financial capacity; fair financing and recovery practices, including a duty to engage qualified collection staff and give them necessary training.

programs.title: Pakistan | Complaint Handling under BC&FRF and SBP Sunwai
programs.why: Under the BC&FRF dispute-resolution pillar, banks must record every complaint, however received, in a complaint management system and keep the records permanently. They must report complaint data to SBP quarterly and give extra care to vulnerable complainants. Customers can escalate through SBP's Sunwai portal. Staff handling complaints must know these steps; no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Complaint recording, retention and quarterly reporting, with extra care for vulnerable complainants.

references.title: Consumer Protection
references.note: SBP's consumer protection and complaint escalation information.

programs.title: Pakistan | Banking Mohtasib Complaints (BCO 1962 Part IVA)
programs.why: Part IVA of the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962 creates the Banking Mohtasib. A customer must first write to the bank; if the bank does not answer or answers unsatisfactorily within 45 days, the customer may complain to the Mohtasib within a further 45 days. Either side may appeal to the SBP Governor within 30 days, and banks must implement the findings within 40 days. Complaint and branch staff should be able to explain this route to customers.

references.title: The Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962
references.note: Establishes the Banking Mohtasib, its jurisdiction, the 45-day prior complaint to the bank, appeals to the SBP Governor and the 40-day implementation period.

programs.title: Pakistan | Mis-selling Prevention and Sales Incentives (BC&FRF)
programs.why: SBP's conduct rules say staff rewards must not encourage behaviour that harms customers, and FTC goals must be part of staff KPIs. For insurance sold through banks, sales quality must weigh at least as much as volume, and staff may not take incentives directly from the product provider. Banks must assess suitability before selling third-party investment products, and the annual training plan must cover SECP's training requirements for selling third-party products. Sales staff need to understand suitability and disclosure.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Rewards must not encourage poor conduct; for insurance sales through banks, quality and quantity of sales carry at least equal weight and staff may not take incentives from product providers.

programs.title: Pakistan | Serving Persons with Disabilities and Vulnerable Consumers (BC&FRF)
programs.why: The BC&FRF requires mandatory awareness and practical training for branch staff on how to serve persons with disabilities, and all employees must know the bank's PWD inclusion policy. Designated model branches must have staff trained in PWD etiquette and at least one staff member with basic sign-language training. Complaints from vulnerable persons must be handled with extra care for how well the complainant can understand the process.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Mandatory awareness and practical training for branch staff on serving persons with disabilities; model branches need staff trained in PWD etiquette and at least one staff member with basic sign-language training.
references.provision: Pillar 6, section 6.1(4); Pillar 3, section 3.3.1; Pillar 5, section 5.1.1.6

programs.title: Pakistan | Customer Data Protection and Secrecy (BC&FRF Pillar 4)
programs.why: Pakistan has no general personal data protection law in force; the bill remains at draft stage. Banks are instead bound by SBP's data protection and privacy pillar in the BC&FRF. It covers consent-based collection, use, sharing, retention and destruction of customer data. SBP also has instructions on keeping customer information secret. Every staff member who handles customer data needs to know these rules.

references.title: Business Conduct & Fair Treatment of Consumers (FTC) Regulatory Framework (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025)
references.note: Data protection and privacy pillar covering the full customer data lifecycle.

references.title: Maintaining fidelity and secrecy of customers' information (BPRD Circular No. 08 of 2018)
references.note: SBP instructions on protecting the confidentiality of customer information.

programs.title: Pakistan | Information Security under SBP ETGRM Framework
programs.why: SBP's Enterprise Technology Governance & Risk Management Framework is the baseline for technology governance, information security and cyber controls at banks, DFIs and MFBs. Senior management must implement it, and the board reviews implementation. Its security controls depend on staff understanding acceptable use and their security duties. No separate general course was verified in the framework text.

references.title: Enterprise Technology Governance & Risk Management Framework for Financial Institutions (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2017)
references.note: Baseline technology governance and cyber security requirements; compliance was due by June 2018.

programs.title: Pakistan | Cyber Security Awareness for Digital and Internet Banking Staff
programs.why: SBP's Regulations for the Security of Internet Banking require employees who operate internet banking systems to have suitable knowledge. They must receive regular training on security risks, controls and monitoring. The same regulations require a formal customer awareness programme. The 2023 digital banking security measures raise the stakes, because banks bear losses when their own response to a fraud is slow.

references.title: Regulations for the Security of Internet Banking
references.issuer: State Bank of Pakistan (Payment Systems Department)
references.note: Relevant staff must have suitable knowledge, and regular training should keep them aware of security risks, controls and monitoring; a formal customer awareness programme is also required.

references.title: Measures to Enhance Security of Digital Banking Products and Services (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2023)
references.note: Digital banking security controls and liability shift.

programs.title: Pakistan | Cyber Risk Management and Incident Response (SBP)
audience: IT risk and operational risk staff
programs.why: SBP expects banks to manage cyber risk through the ETGRM framework. Its cyber instructions require banks to test incident response and continuity plans and to record cyber attacks and breaches for SBP review. SBP supervises cyber governance and incident response and expects significant incidents to be reported and fixed promptly. In January 2026 SBP and the Pakistan Banks Association ran an industry-wide cyber simulation.

references.title: Enterprise Technology Governance & Risk Management Framework for Financial Institutions (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2017)
BPRD Circular No. 07 of 2016
references.note: Cyber security instructions requiring tested incident response and continuity plans and records of cyber attacks.

references.title: Banking Regulation and Supervision
references.note: SBP reviews cyber governance and incident response and expects timely reporting of significant incidents.

programs.title: Pakistan | Cyber Incident Escalation and Reporting to SBP
programs.why: SBP supervisors expect significant cyber incidents to be reported and fixed promptly, and banks must keep records of cyber attacks for inspection. Staff need to recognise an incident and escalate it fast. No public reporting deadline for banks was confirmed in the sources reviewed.

references.title: Banking Regulation and Supervision
references.note: SBP monitors significant cyber incidents and requires timely reporting and remediation.

references.title: BPRD Circular No. 07 of 2016
references.note: Records of cyber attacks and breaches to be kept available for SBP.

programs.title: Pakistan | ICT Risk Management and Cloud Outsourcing (SBP)
programs.why: The ETGRM framework sets SBP's baseline for technology risk governance. SBP's 2023 cloud outsourcing framework adds requirements for using cloud service providers. IT and risk staff need working knowledge of both, though neither prescribes a separate course.

references.title: Enterprise Technology Governance & Risk Management Framework for Financial Institutions (BPRD Circular No. 05 of 2017)
Framework on Outsourcing to Cloud Service Providers (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2023)
references.note: Requirements for banks using cloud service providers.

programs.title: Pakistan | Basel III Liquidity Standards (LCR and NSFR)
programs.why: SBP's Basel III liquidity standards require banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to keep the Liquidity Coverage Ratio at or above 100% and to meet the Net Stable Funding Ratio, with monitoring tools such as maturity mismatch and funding concentration. A fall below the minimum must be reported to SBP at once. Treasury, risk and reporting staff need to know the calculations, but no training is prescribed.

references.title: Basel III: Liquidity Standards (BPRD Circular No. 08 of 2016)
references.note: LCR and NSFR rules with a 100% LCR floor after phase-in, immediate notification to SBP if the LCR falls short, and supplementary liquidity monitoring tools.

programs.title: Pakistan | Basel Capital Adequacy Framework (SBP Basel III)
audience: Credit staff who assign risk weights
programs.why: Banks and DFIs compute capital adequacy under SBP's Basel III instructions. In September 2025 SBP issued revised standardized-approach instructions for credit risk weighted assets, run in parallel for four quarters from September 30, 2025 to June 30, 2026 before final rules replace the 2006 credit risk chapter. Staff who classify exposures and prepare CAR returns need to understand the rules; no training duty is stated.

references.title: Basel Capital Adequacy Framework: Instructions for Credit Risk (September 24, 2025; BPRD Circular No. 03 of 2025)
references.note: Revised standardized approach for credit risk RWAs, applied on a parallel-run basis from September 30, 2025 to June 30, 2026, with extra time for quarterly CAR statements.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Framework for Risk Management in Outsourcing Arrangements
programs.why: SBP's outsourcing framework, revised in 2019, requires due diligence on providers, including their business continuity arrangements. Contracts must include continuity and data protection terms. Banks must monitor providers and report material adverse developments to SBP within two working days. Staff who manage outsourcing need to be competent in these rules.

references.title: Framework for Risk Management in Outsourcing Arrangements by Financial Institutions (revisions under BPRD Circular No. 06 of 2019)
references.note: Provider due diligence, contract terms, monitoring and notification to SBP within two working days of material adverse developments.

programs.title: Pakistan | Business Continuity and Contingency Planning (SBP)
programs.why: SBP requires contingency plans based on realistic disruption scenarios to be in place and tested periodically, including for outsourced services. Banks must also test their cyber incident response and continuity plans. Staff with continuity roles must know their part in these tests.

references.title: Framework for Risk Management in Outsourcing Arrangements by Financial Institutions (revisions under BPRD Circular No. 06 of 2019)
references.note: Contingency plans tested periodically; providers' disaster recovery testing to be monitored.

references.title: BPRD Circular No. 07 of 2016
references.note: Testing of incident response and business continuity plans.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Regulatory Framework on Recovery Planning
programs.why: BPRD Circular No. 02 of 2025 (July 2025) set SBP's expectations for bank recovery plans, which banks may scale to their size and complexity. According to SBP's circular index, the first board-approved plans were due by June 30, 2026. The framework text itself could not be opened (SBP's circular pages block automated access), so this is recorded as a governance competence without a verified training duty.

references.title: Regulatory Framework on Recovery Planning (BPRD Circular No. 02 of 2025)
references.note: SBP circular page; blocked automated access, so the framework text was not opened.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking
programs.why: SBP's Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking set exposure limits, financial analysis conditions, security and margin rules, monitoring, guarantees and operational rules for banks and DFIs. Lending staff must apply them on every facility, so credit officers need working knowledge of the regulations, but the regulations do not prescribe training.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking (updated June 2024)
references.note: Per-party and group exposure limits, financial statement requirements, security and margin rules and post-disbursement monitoring.

programs.title: Pakistan | Classification of Loans and Subjective Evaluation (SBP PRs)
programs.why: Under the Prudential Regulations, banks classify loans on time-based criteria and must also make a subjective evaluation of performing and non-performing accounts, downgrading where the borrower's cash flow, account conduct, security or documentation warrant it. Staff who monitor credit need to apply both tests consistently. No training is prescribed.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking (updated June 2024)
references.note: Time-based classification criteria plus a required subjective evaluation that can downgrade any account, including a performing one.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for SME Financing (updated July 16, 2026)
references.note: Separate classification and provisioning criteria for SME loans.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Guidelines on NPLs Management Strategy
programs.why: SBP's 2024 guidelines require banks to have a defined strategy for identifying, managing, monitoring and reducing non-performing loans, with limits on NPL ageing, dedicated workout units separate from origination, clear authority matrices and fair treatment of borrowers. They refer to staff expertise as an operational capacity to assess, but set no training duty.

references.title: Guidelines for NPLs Management Strategy (Annexure A to BPRD Circular No. 03 of 2024)
references.note: Banks must put an NPL strategy in place; workout units should be separate from loan origination and consumer protection must be considered.

programs.title: Pakistan | Rescheduling and Restructuring of Loans (SBP PRs)
programs.why: The Prudential Regulations allow rescheduling or restructuring under board-approved policy but forbid doing it simply to avoid classification. A restructured non-performing loan can be upgraded only after set cash recoveries and a period of performance, and the rules differ for corporate, SME and consumer loans. Staff must know which conditions apply; no training duty is set.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking (updated June 2024)
references.note: Upgrade only after terms are met for at least one year and part of the restructured amount is recovered; restructuring must not be used to avoid classification.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for SME Financing (updated July 16, 2026)
references.note: SME loans may be upgraded after 10% cash recovery and six months of compliance, or at once on 35% recovery.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing (updated August 3, 2016)
references.note: Consumer facilities need a written rescheduling policy and limits on how often a facility can be restructured.

programs.title: Pakistan | Credit Information Bureau (eCIB) Checks and Reporting
programs.why: Before approving, renewing or restructuring credit, banks must obtain a recent credit report from SBP's eCIB or a licensed credit bureau (for corporate lending, no older than two months) and document why they lend to borrowers with overdues. Consumer lenders must join at least one consumer credit bureau. Staff need to read and act on these reports, but no training is required.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Corporate/Commercial Banking (updated June 2024)
references.note: CIB report must be weighed for every exposure and must not be older than two months at approval.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for SME Financing (updated July 16, 2026)
references.note: eCIB or licensed bureau report required for all SME proposals, including renewals and restructurings.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing (updated August 3, 2016)
references.note: Consumer lenders must be members of a consumer credit information bureau and use the eCIB co-borrower utility.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing
audience: Credit card and auto finance staff
programs.why: The consumer financing regulations cover debt-burden limits, documentation, recovery procedures, bureau membership and restructuring for personal loans, cards, auto and housing finance. They encourage institutions to give their staff ongoing training on consumer finance, but stop short of requiring it, so this is a competence area with recommended ongoing training.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing (updated August 3, 2016)
references.note: Institutions starting consumer finance are encouraged to give staff sufficient training on an ongoing basis.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Prudential Regulations for Housing Finance (2026)
programs.why: In 2026 SBP issued separate Prudential Regulations for Housing Finance (updated August 18, 2026) under its SME, Housing and Sustainable Finance Department. They set eligibility, documentation, security and risk management rules for mortgage lending. Mortgage staff need to know them; no training duty was found in the text.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Housing Finance (updated August 18, 2026)
references.note: Housing finance rules issued with SH&SFD Circular No. 04 of 2026, including standard document checklists for salaried and self-employed borrowers.

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Prudential Regulations for SME Financing (2026)
programs.why: The SME regulations, updated on July 16, 2026, require a board-approved SME strategy, in-house or outsourced business analysis capacity, a dedicated SME function headed by a person with at least five years of SME finance experience, a CEO-chaired SME committee and digital processes. These are capacity and experience requirements rather than a training rule.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for SME Financing (updated July 16, 2026)
references.provision: Regulations R-1 to R-4 and R-14
references.note: SME strategy, business analysis capacity, a head of SME with at least five years of experience, a management committee and digitalisation of SME finance.

programs.title: Pakistan | Agriculture Financing: Qualified Agri Staff and Livestock Inspections
programs.why: SBP's agriculture financing regulations require a dedicated agri finance unit staffed with qualified agri financing experts and officers. Where livestock is the main security, banks must inspect it at least twice a year, and the inspections must be done by a qualified and appropriately trained person. Staff doing these inspections therefore need specific training.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Agriculture Financing (updated February 12, 2024)
references.note: Agri policy must provide for a dedicated unit with qualified experts (R-1); livestock inspections at least twice a year by a qualified and appropriately trained person (R-17).

programs.title: Pakistan | Microfinance Banks: Microenterprise Lending Capacity (SBP PRs for MFBs)
programs.why: Microfinance banks that want to make microenterprise loans (up to Rs. 5 million) must first build institutional capacity, which the regulations say includes product manuals, credit risk systems, controls and trainings, and must have a board-approved microenterprise lending policy. Training of the lending staff is therefore an express precondition for this business.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Microfinance Banks (updated May 16, 2025)
references.note: MFBs must develop institutional capacity, including trainings, before extending microenterprise loans.

programs.title: Pakistan | Fair Debt Collection and Recovery Staff (SBP PRs for MFBs)
programs.why: SBP's microfinance bank regulations set conduct rules for collection: no contact at inconvenient times, disclosure of identity, recorded calls, no harassment of family members and protection of borrower data. MFBs must have a code of conduct for recovery staff, engage suitably qualified collection staff and give them necessary training. The express training rule applies to microfinance banks; commercial banks are covered by the general BC&FRF conduct rules.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Microfinance Banks (updated May 16, 2025)
references.note: MFBs must frame a code of lawful conduct for recovery staff and engage suitably qualified collection staff with necessary training.

references.title: Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing (updated August 3, 2016)
references.note: Banks/DFIs must have documented recovery procedures with objective triggers for delinquent consumer loans.

programs.title: Pakistan | Unclaimed Deposits under BCO 1962 Section 31
programs.why: Section 31 of the Banking Companies Ordinance treats deposits, unpaid instruments and safe-custody items with no customer activity for ten years as unclaimed. Banks must give notice to the customer, report the amounts in the prescribed return and surrender them to SBP. Branch and deposit staff need to track inactive accounts correctly; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962
references.note: Ten-year inactivity test for deposits, instruments and safe-custody articles, and the procedure for surrendering unclaimed amounts to SBP.

programs.title: Pakistan | Wire Transfer Rules under SBP AML/CFT/CPF Regulations
programs.why: SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations require complete originator and beneficiary information on domestic and cross-border wire transfers, and set duties for ordering, intermediary and beneficiary institutions when information is missing. Payment staff must apply these checks; general AML training covers them but no separate wire-transfer training is set.

references.title: AML/CFT/CPF Regulations (consolidated, updated to 28 November 2022)
references.note: Sets the information that must travel with domestic and cross-border wire transfers and the duties of ordering, intermediary and beneficiary institutions.

programs.title: Pakistan | Payment Systems and Electronic Fund Transfers Act 2007
programs.why: The PS&EFT Act gives SBP power over payment systems and sets consumer rules for electronic fund transfers: disclosure of terms, notice of changes, periodic statements, error investigation and correction, consumer liability limits, secrecy, and offences for electronic fraud. Staff handling EFT disputes need to know these rules; the Act sets no training duty.

references.title: Payment Systems and Electronic Fund Transfers Act, 2007
references.note: Error notification and correction (sections 36-38), consumer liability (section 40), and secrecy and privacy (section 70).

programs.title: Pakistan | SBP Regulations for Payment Card Security
programs.why: SBP's payment card security regulations require card service providers, including banks, to run a card security framework with risk assessment, EMV cards, anti-skimming devices, transaction alerts and a consumer awareness programme. They also require banks to train merchants on security measures for card transactions, such as checking a customer's CNIC, so acquiring staff must be able to deliver that training. The express training duty in s.4(k) is to train merchants, not the bank's own staff, so staff training is classified as competence.

references.title: Regulations for Payment Card Security (PSD Circular No. 05 of 2016)
references.note: Card service providers must train merchants on POS security measures and run a formal consumer awareness programme.

programs.title: Pakistan | Branchless Banking Agents: Capacity Building (SBP BB Regulations)
programs.why: SBP's Branchless Banking Regulations require authorised institutions to take adequate measures to build agents' capacity through training, particularly on money laundering and terrorist financing risks, alongside customer outreach, fraud detection and complaint handling. Banks offering branchless banking must therefore train their agents and the staff who manage them.

references.title: Branchless Banking Regulations (revised December 30, 2019; BPRD Circular No. 10 of 2019)
references.note: Institutions must build agents' capacity through trainings, especially on ML/TF risks and their implications.

programs.title: Pakistan | Home Remittances via Branchless Banking and the FE Manual
audience: Branchless banking agents serving remittance accounts
programs.why: For Home Remittance Accounts, banks must ensure that branchless banking agents are properly trained to serve customers, along with biometric checks and agent due diligence. The FE Manual also tells banks to train relevant head-office and branch staff on issuing and verifying electronic proceeds realization certificates for inward remittances so they can guide customers.

references.title: Branchless Banking Regulations (revised December 30, 2019; BPRD Circular No. 10 of 2019)
references.note: Banks must ensure agents are properly trained to serve HRA customers.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 10: Inward and Outward Remittances
references.provision: Annexure on e-PRC and S-PRC guidelines, paragraph 12
references.note: Authorized Dealers to acquaint or train relevant staff on issuing and verifying e-PRCs and S-PRCs.

programs.title: Pakistan | Foreign Exchange Manual: Capacity Building of Authorized Dealer Staff
audience: Foreign exchange staff at authorized branches
programs.why: Chapter 2 of SBP's Foreign Exchange Manual requires Authorized Dealers to have a board-approved training and development policy for foreign exchange work. At the start of each calendar year they must assess every relevant employee's FX training needs, set focus areas such as trade, foreign currency accounts and remittances, include AML/CFT and IT topics, cover remote branches, and assess staff after training.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 2: Authorized Dealers
references.note: Board-approved FX training policy; annual training-needs assessment for each related employee at the start of the calendar year; post-training assessment.

programs.title: Pakistan | Foreign Exchange Services to Individuals (FE Manual)
programs.why: Banks must offer travel, education and medical foreign exchange services at all authorized branches. The FE Manual requires that officials dealing with customers for these services, including contact-centre staff, are adequately trained in foreign exchange business and know the applicable rules, and that a head-office focal person is appointed.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 2: Authorized Dealers
references.note: Officials serving individuals for FX needs, including call-centre staff, must be adequately trained and know the rules.

programs.title: Pakistan | Anti-Harassment Policy for Listed Banks (SECP CCG)
programs.why: In 2024 SECP amended the Code of Corporate Governance so that boards of listed companies, including listed banks, must ensure an anti-harassment policy is in place. SECP said the change supports compliance with the 2010 harassment Act. Staff need to know the policy for it to work, but no training is prescribed.

references.title: S.R.O. 920(I)/2024 Amendments to the Listed Companies (Code of Corporate Governance) Regulations, 2019
references.issuer: Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
references.note: Board to ensure an anti-harassment policy; also adds sustainability and DE&I duties.

programs.title: Pakistan | Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010
programs.why: The Act requires every organisation to adopt the statutory Code of Conduct and form a three-member inquiry committee that includes at least one woman. The code must be displayed in English and in a language most employees understand. The 2022 amendment widened the definitions of harassment and employee and added former employees as possible complainants. The display duty is an awareness measure; no formal training requirement was verified.

references.title: The Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010
references.issuer: Pakistan Code (Ministry of Law and Justice)
references.note: Code of Conduct, inquiry committee and duty to display the code at the workplace.

references.title: Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace (Amendment) Act, 2022
references.issuer: Federal Ombudsperson for Protection against Harassment
references.note: Broadened the definitions of harassment and employee and extended protection to gig, part-time and former workers.

programs.title: Pakistan | IFRS 9 Expected Credit Loss under SBP Application Instructions
programs.why: Banks, DFIs and MFBs apply IFRS 9 under SBP's application instructions (BPRD Circular No. 03 of 2022, later amended, including in January 2025). The opened parallel-reporting version advised institutions to train credit risk and finance teams for transition and ongoing application, and expected internal audit to be sufficiently skilled. The final 2022 text sits on an SBP path that blocks automated access, so the training advice could not be confirmed in force and this stays at competence.

references.title: IFRS 9 Application Instructions for Parallel Reporting (BPRD Circular Letter No. 24 of 2021)
references.note: Draft for parallel reporting, later replaced. It advised training credit risk and finance teams and required skilled internal audit review of ECL models.

references.title: IFRS 9 Application Instructions (BPRD Circular No. 03 of 2022)
references.note: Final instructions; host blocked automated access, not opened.

programs.title: Pakistan | FATCA Due Diligence and FBR AEOI Enrolment
programs.why: Pakistani banks collect FATCA self-declarations at onboarding. They register with the IRS, and FBR's AEOI portal enrols reporting entities for FATCA, CRS and CbC reporting. SBP's 2014 instructions told banks to register with the IRS while the intergovernmental agreement was pending. Account-opening and reporting staff need to know these steps, but no training obligation exists.

references.title: Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) (BPRD Circular Letter No. 16 of 2014)
references.note: Allowed banks to register with the IRS as participating FFIs while the intergovernmental agreement was pending.

references.title: Enrol for FATCA, CRS & CbC
references.note: FBR enrolment portal for reporting financial institutions.

programs.title: Pakistan | Common Reporting Standard under Income Tax Rules Chapter XIIA
programs.why: Pakistan's CRS rules are in Chapter XIIA of the Income Tax Rules 2002. They require financial institutions to identify reportable accounts through due diligence and to file with FBR each year. FBR can register non-compliant institutions compulsorily and audit them. FBR's guidance note and AEOI implementation manual explain what reporting institutions must do. Staff need to apply them correctly, though no training is prescribed.

references.title: Guidance Note on Common Reporting Standard for Automatic Exchange of Financial Account Information
references.note: Explains CRS due diligence and reporting under the rules inserted by S.R.O. 166(I)/2017.

references.title: Circular No. 14 of 2022: AEOI Implementation Manual
references.note: Compliance steps for reporting financial institutions, including compulsory registration of non-registered institutions and the 30 May annual deadline for CRS returns.

references.title: Common Reporting Standard (CRS) Rules (BPRD Circular Letter No. 10 of 2017)
references.note: SBP passed the CRS rules on to banks for compliance.

programs.title: Pakistan | Trade Finance under the FE Manual (Imports and Exports)
audience: Authorized branch staff handling LCs and collections
programs.why: Import and export payments run through Authorized Dealers under Chapters 12 and 13 of the FE Manual. Chapter 2 requires the annual training-needs assessment for FX staff and names international trade as a training focus area, with AML/CFT built into function-specific modules. Trade staff therefore fall under an express FX training requirement.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 2: Authorized Dealers
references.note: International trade is named as a training focus; AML/CFT must be part of FX training modules.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 13: Imports
references.note: Rules Authorized Dealers apply when handling import payments and documents.

references.title: Foreign Exchange Manual, Chapter 12: Exports
references.note: Rules for export documentation and realization of proceeds.

programs.title: Pakistan | Digital Onboarding and Biometric Verification (SBP Onboarding Framework)
programs.why: SBP's Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework allows digital onboarding for residents and non-residents, with NADRA biometric verification (or Verisys where biometrics are not possible), liveness detection, video KYC record retention and security requirements. Before launch, the compliance officer and CISO must confirm readiness in writing. Staff running digital onboarding need to know these controls; no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2025)
references.note: Biometric/Verisys identity verification, digital onboarding for all customer types and security and infrastructure requirements in Section K.

notes: October 2025: SBP issued the BC&FRF (BPRD Circular No. 04 of 2025). Per SBP's circular page (not opened in this check), it withdraws the circulars in its Annexure-A and its governance pillar applied from 1 January 2026. The framework text still requires banks to apply the 2016 Conduct Assessment Framework (BC&CPD Circular No. 3 of 2016), so that was not withdrawn. Check Annexure-A before citing older consumer circulars.

SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations (2020) were amended in January 2021 and November 2022; the text cited here is SBP's consolidated version updated to 28 November 2022, which warns that later circulars may change it. Related instructions came in July 2025 (Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework, BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2025) and April 2026 (BPRD Circular Letter No. 10 of 2026 on accounts for licensed virtual asset service providers). Check SBP for a newer consolidated text.

AML Act 2010: the 2020 amendments put CDD duties into sections 7A-7D, changed the STR deadline to 'promptly' and raised penalties. A 2023 Act created a National AML/CFT Authority. Pakistan Code also lists a 2025 version of that Act marked 'under final review', so its status should be checked.

FMU: the Suspicious Transaction and Currency Transaction Reporting Regulations 2025 (November 2025, under section 44 of the AML Act) repealed the AML Regulations 2015, keep prompt STR filing through goAML and set a seven-working-day CTR deadline. FMU's 2026 circulars added red flags for corruption-related money laundering (No. 01, 24 June 2026) and STR-G reporting for government entities (No. 02, 28 July 2026).

Pakistan still has no general personal data protection law in force (the Personal Data Protection Bill drafts remain unpassed), so customer data rules for banks come mainly from the BC&FRF data protection pillar. The Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act 2025 created a Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority but adds no bank training duties.

In 2025 SBP issued a Technology Risk Management Framework for payment institutions (EMIs, PSOs, PSPs), with compliance due by March 2026. Banks remain under the 2017 ETGRM framework; no newer bank-wide cyber framework was found.
